title: Shadow English Practice Day 3 | English Speaking Practice for Beginners | Speak English Fluently

sentences.t: Hello and welcome back to Leo English podcast.
We're very happy to see you here today.
I'm Tina.
And I'm Leo.
On this channel, we help you learn English through natural conversation, useful daily expressions, and simple speaking practice you can use right away.
And today, we have a very useful lesson for beginners.
That's right. Today's lesson is shadow English practice day three.
We focus on speaking practice for beginners and we help you speak more fluently step by step.
If you understand English a little, but speaking still feels slow, this lesson is for you.
We show you how to shadow, how to repeat naturally, and how to feel more comfortable with real English.
So, if you want more confidence, better rhythm, and smoother speaking, stay with us.
And if you enjoy learning with us, please like this video and subscribe to the channel.
Don't forget to click the bell, too.
That way, you never miss a new lesson.
Okay, I'm ready.
Great. Let's get started.
How are you today, Leo?
I'm pretty good.
I'm a little sleepy, but good.
Why are you sleepy?
I stayed up too late last night.
I listened to English audio and then I listened to one more and then one more.
So, you study hard.
Well, I study for 20 minutes and then I become curious.
Curious about what?
About everything. One short English video becomes seven short English videos.
That sounds very familiar.
How are you today?
I'm good. I feel organized today.
I write my to-do list at 7:15, I make coffee at 7:25, and I start work at 8:00.
Wow, your morning sounds like a train schedule.
Thank you. I think that is a compliment.
It is. My morning sounds more like a comedy show.
What do you do this weekend?
On Saturday, I meet a friend for lunch.
We talk for almost 90 minutes.
On Sunday, I clean my room for 30 minutes and then reward myself with a snack for 60 minutes.
That is not a fair time balance.
I know, but I believe in emotional support snacks.
I have a quieter weekend.
I read a short article, I call my sister, and I practice some short English sentences out loud.
Really? What kind of sentences?
Short daily sentences.
Things like, "I'm on my way."
"That sounds good."
And, "Can you say that again?"
Speaking of short daily sentences, that sounds a lot like shadow practice.
Exactly. Today's topic is perfect for that.
Good, because I think many beginners want to speak, but they don't know how to start.
Yes, and shadowing is one very helpful way to start.
So, let's talk about it together.
Okay, Leo. Let's begin with the most basic question.
What is shadow English practice?
Shadow English practice is when you listen to English and repeat it very quickly after the speaker.
Exactly. You listen, you follow, and you copy the sound, the rhythm, and the sentence pattern.
Wait, what does rhythm mean here?
Good question. Rhythm is the natural beat of the language.
Some words sound stronger and some sound softer.
So, shadowing is not only saying the words, it is also copying the music of English.
That is a very nice way to say it.
I like shadowing because it feels active.
I'm not just sitting there and staring at a page.
That is one big benefit.
Shadowing keeps your mouth, ears, and brain working together.
I think that helps beginners a lot.
Sometimes beginners understand more than they can say.
Very true. Many learners know basic words, but when they try to speak, they stop too often.
Yes, they know go, eat, want, and like, but the sentence still feels difficult.
Shadowing helps because it gives them full sentences to copy.
They do not build every sentence from zero.
So, instead of thinking word by word, they practice sentence by sentence.
Exactly. For example, if you hear, "I usually drink coffee in the morning."
You repeat the whole sentence.
Then your mouth learns that pattern.
And later I can change it.
I can say, "I usually drink tea in the morning."
Perfect. That is how practice becomes personal.
Is shadowing good only for pronunciation?
No, not only for pronunciation.
It also helps listening, speaking speed, memory, confidence, and sentence patterns.
That's a lot from one activity.
Yes, and that is why it is so useful.
I think beginners sometimes feel scared because native speakers talk fast.
Yes, that is common.
But shadowing teaches your ears to hear common patterns again and again.
So, the language becomes less scary because it feels more familiar.
Exactly. Familiar language feels easier to understand and easier to use.
Okay, then what is day three practice?
Is it harder than day one?
Usually, day three means learners already know the basic idea.
So, now they need more rhythm, more comfort, and a little more control.
Not too hard, but not too easy.
Right. We want practice that feels possible, but still useful.
What kind of sentences should beginners shadow on day three?
Simple daily life sentences are best.
Short sentences about routines, feelings, plans, food, work, school, family, and free time.
Can you give examples?
Of course. I get up at 7:00 a.m.
every day. I'm a little tired today.
I need to buy a few things after work.
That sounds like a good idea.
Can you help me with this?
Those are great because I can actually use them.
Exactly. Real use matters a lot.
I think one mistake is choosing sentences that are too long.
Yes, that is a very common mistake.
Beginners should not start with long speeches or very advanced topics.
So, not the economic situation becomes increasingly complicated.
No, that is not a beginner sentence.
Good, because I don't even say that in my first language.
A better sentence is things are getting more expensive.
It's shorter, clearer, and more useful.
What is the best way to do shadow practice?
I like a simple five-step method.
Good, I need numbers.
My brain likes numbers.
Step one, listen to the sentence one time.
Just listen, no speaking yet.
Right. Step two, listen again and read the words if you have a transcript.
That helps me notice the full sentence.
Step three, repeat after the speaker.
This is the real shadow part.
Yes. Step four, repeat again, but try to copy the rhythm and emotion more closely.
So, if the speaker sounds relaxed, I try to sound relaxed, too.
Exactly. Step five, say the sentence alone without the audio.
Ah, that part is scary, but helpful.
Yes, because it shows what you remember.
How long should one practice session be?
For beginners, 10 to 15 minutes is enough.
Even 8 minutes can help if you do it regularly.
That is good news.
Some people think they need 1 hour.
No, short, regular practice is often better.
How many sentences should beginners practice in one session?
About 5 to 10 sentences is fine.
It depends on sentence length and your energy.
So, five strong sentences are better than 30 weak sentences.
Exactly right.
I also think people go too fast.
They press play, repeat badly, and move on.
Yes, slow practice is often smart practice.
Wait, what does move on mean?
Move on means go to the next thing.
In this case, it means stop practicing one sentence and start another sentence.
Got it. So, don't move on too quickly.
Exactly. Stay with a sentence until it feels comfortable.
What if a learner cannot catch every word?
That is okay.
First, listen for the general sound.
Then, listen again.
Then, check the transcript if possible.
So, confusion at the beginning is normal.
Very normal. Beginners should not panic after one listen.
I like that advice.
Sometimes learners think, "I don't get it, so I'm bad at English."
Yes, but that idea is not true.
Listening takes time.
Your ears need training.
Like exercise.
Exactly. Nobody lifts a heavy weight perfectly on the first day.
Definitely not.
Another useful tip is to practice one feeling at a time.
What do you mean by that?
Practice relaxed sentences, happy sentences, surprised sentences, and polite questions.
English changes a little with feeling.
Oh, that's interesting.
So, really can sound different in different situations.
Yes. Really can sound excited, surprised, confused, or doubtful.
English is dramatic.
Yes, sometimes.
Can we show our viewers a short shadow example?
Great idea. Let's do a few simple lines.
I'm on my way.
I'm on my way.
Sorry, I'm a little late.
Sorry, I'm a little late.
No problem. Take your time.
No problem. Take your time.
Do you want coffee or tea?
Do you want coffee or tea?
I think I'll have tea.
I think I'll have tea.
Very good. Those lines are short, natural, and easy to use in life.
And they feel much easier than random textbook sentences.
Yes, because they connect to real situations.
Should learners practice with slow audio or normal audio?
Beginners can start with slightly slower audio, but normal, natural audio is also very useful if the sentences are clear and short.
So, the sentence choice matters more than the speed sometimes.
Exactly. A short, clear sentence at normal speed can be easier than a long, confusing sentence at slow speed.
That makes sense.
Also, I tell learners to repeat one audio clip for several days.
Really? The same clip?
Yes. Repetition builds comfort.
Day one feels hard.
Day two feels better.
Day three feels more natural.
Ah, now day three makes more sense.
Yes. Day three is where some fluency starts to appear.
Not perfect fluency.
No, of course not, but a a feeling of control.
I beginners also ask this, "Should I understand every word before I shadow?"
Not always every word, but you should understand the main meaning.
Shadowing without meaning is much weaker.
So meaning comes first, then repetition becomes more powerful.
Exactly. If you know what you are saying, your brain remembers it better.
What if someone feels embarrassed speaking out loud?
That is common, too.
They can practice quietly at first.
They can also practice in a room alone, during a walk, or even in a parked car.
The car classroom.
Yes, very practical.
I sometimes practice English while washing dishes.
That works, too, as long as you can focus.
Sometimes I repeat a sentence three times, and then I forget it 5 minutes later.
That means you may need active review.
After shadowing, try saying the sentence later without looking.
So not only copy, but also recall.
Exactly. Recall is very important.
Wait, what does recall mean?
Recall means remember and bring it back from your memory.
Got it. So I hear it, I say it, and later I try to recall it.
Perfect. Can shadowing help grammar, too?
Yes, very much.
You see and hear grammar inside real sentences.
For example, "I usually go."
"She doesn't like."
"Are you coming later?"
So grammar becomes a habit, not only a rule.
Exactly. That is one reason shadowing feels natural.
I like that.
Some learners get tired of grammar charts.
Charts can help, but real sentences help, too.
What are the biggest shadowing mistakes?
I see five common mistakes.
One, using sentences that are too difficult.
Two, speaking too softly to hear yourself.
Three, practicing once and then stopping.
Four, ignoring meaning.
Five, trying to sound perfect immediately.
That last one is a big one.
Yes, beginners do not need perfection.
They need repetition and comfort.
So, if my voice sounds strange at first, that is normal.
Very normal. New sounds often feel strange before they feel natural.
That makes me feel better.
Good. Another helpful tip is to record yourself once or twice a week.
Oof, that sounds scary, too.
It can feel uncomfortable, but it helps.
You can notice your pace, your clarity, and your improvement.
I recorded myself last month, and I noticed one thing.
What is that?
I pause every three words like I'm climbing a mountain.
And now?
Now I pause less.
Still not perfect, but better.
That is real progress.
I think beginners need to hear that.
Better is enough.
Better matters.
Yes, improvement is more important than perfection.
Can shadowing become a daily habit?
Absolutely. A very simple routine works well.
For example, practice at 8:30 every evening for 10 minutes.
That sounds realistic.
Or practice after breakfast every morning.
Habit grows faster when it has a regular place in your day.
I like evening practice because my day feels quieter then.
I prefer morning practice because my mind feels fresh.
See, we're different.
And that is okay.
The best time is the time you can keep.
That is a very important point.
Also, learners should choose topics they enjoy.
Food, travel, school, daily routines, hobbies, feelings, shopping, family.
Yes, if I enjoy the topic, I repeat more willingly.
Exactly. Interest helps repetition.
Can we talk about one beginner shadow routine from beginning to end?
Sure. Let's imagine a learner named Anna.
At 7:00 p.m., Anna opens a short audio lesson.
It has six daily life sentences.
First, she listens one time.
Then, she listens again with the text.
After that, she repeats sentence one three times.
Yes, then she repeats sentence two three times, and so on.
Then, she goes back and says all six sentences again.
Exactly. After that, she chooses two sentences she likes most and says them from memory.
Then, maybe she changes them a little.
Very good. For example, "I'm a little tired today" becomes "I'm a little busy today."
That is smart.
Same pattern, new word.
Yes. Finally, Anna says one sentence later that night in real life, maybe to a friend or to herself.
That feels very practical and possible.
That is the goal.
I think the big message is this: shadowing is simple, but simple does not mean weak.
Exactly. Simple practice done often creates strong results.
So, day three is not about doing something magical.
It is about building comfort with natural English.
Very well said.
Thank you. I learned something, too.
We all do.
You know, Leo, while we were talking, we used many useful words and phrases.
Let's study them together now.
Yes, please. My brain likes a nice, clear review.
First word, shadow.
In this lesson, shadow means listen and repeat after a speaker very quickly.
Oh, yes. Not the dark shape on the ground.
Exactly. For example, I shadow short English sentences every evening.
Another example is shadow practice helps me copy natural speech.
And you can also say, I shadow podcasts for 10 minutes after dinner.
A tip is to shadow short, clear audio first.
What do you like to shadow?
I like to shadow daily conversations because they feel useful.
Next word, rhythm.
This means the natural beat or flow of spoken English.
Oh, yes. This one is important.
English has a sound pattern.
Exactly. For example, I try to copy the rhythm of the sentence.
Another example is her rhythm sounds natural and calm.
And you can also say, my rhythm gets better when I practice slowly first.
A related word is pace.
Rhythm is not only speed.
What helps your rhythm most?
Repeating the same sentence many times helps my rhythm most.
Next phrase, move on.
This means go to the next thing.
Oh, yes. I move on too quickly sometimes.
Exactly. For example, don't move on before the sentence feels comfortable.
Another example is we finish one line, then we move on.
And you can also say, I want to move on, but I need one more try.
A common mistake is moving on too early.
When do you move on too quickly?
I move on too quickly when I feel impatient.
Next word, recall.
This means remember something and bring it back later.
Oh, yes. This is hard for me.
Exactly. For example, I shadow the sentence first, then I recall it later.
Another example is recall helps turn practice into memory.
And you can also say, I can recall three sentences from yesterday's lesson.
A good is to test yourself after a short break.
What helps you recall better?
Saying the sentence again before bed helps me recall better.
Next word, pace.
This means speed, especially the speed of speaking.
Oh, yes. Some learners want a fast pace too soon.
Exactly. For example, my pace is slow, but clear.
Another example is good pace matters more than rushing.
And you can also say, I need a slower pace when I learn new sounds.
The opposite of slow pace is fast pace.
What pace feels best for you?
A medium pace feels best because I can still think clearly.
Next phrase, from memory.
This means without reading or listening in that moment.
Oh, yes. That part shows the truth.
Exactly. For example, I shadow two sentences from memory after practice.
Another example is speaking from memory helps build confidence.
And you can also say, I can say that line from memory now.
A tip is to start with just one or two lines from memory.
What sentence can you say from memory today?
I can say, I'm on my way from memory very easily.
Next phrase, daily habit.
This means something you do every day or almost every day.
Oh, yes. Shadowing works better as a daily habit.
Exactly. For example, 10 minutes of practice becomes a strong daily habit.
Another example is my daily habit is listening after breakfast.
And you can also say, a small daily habit is easier to keep.
That is a great tip.
What daily habit do you want to build?
I want to build a daily habit of speaking out loud at night.
Next word, comfortable.
This means relaxed, natural, and not too stressed.
Oh, yes. I want English to feel comfortable, not scary.
Exactly. For example, I practice one sentence until it feels comfortable.
Another example is I feel comfortable with short greetings now.
And you can also say, "I'm more comfortable when I know the meaning."
The opposite is uncomfortable.
What makes you feel comfortable in practice?
Clear audio and short sentences make me feel comfortable.
Next word, repeat.
This means say something again.
Oh, yes. This is the heart of shadowing.
Exactly. For example, I repeat the line three times.
Another example is, "Please repeat that more slowly."
And you can also say, "I repeat useful phrases during my walk."
A tip is to repeat with attention, not only with speed.
What do you repeat most often?
I repeat polite questions most often because I use them a lot.
Next phrase, real life.
This means normal everyday situations outside study time.
Oh, yes. That's why useful sentences matter.
Exactly. For example, I want English I can use in real life.
Another example is, "This phrase helps me in real life at cafes."
And you can also say, "Real life English is easier to remember because it feels practical."
A common mistake is learning sentences with no real-life use.
What real-life topic do you like most?
I like travel English most because I want to use it someday.
Great. Now, let's review all the words and phrases together.
Yes, summary time.
Shadow, listen and repeat after a speaker quickly.
Rhythm, the natural beat or flow of spoken English.
Move on, go to the next thing.
Recall, remember something later.
Pace, the speed of speaking.
From memory, without reading or listening in that moment.
Daily habit, something you do everyday or regularly.
Comfortable, relaxed and natural, not too stressed.
Repeat, say something again.
Real life, normal everyday situations outside study time.
Okay Leo, that was a lot of talking about shadow English practice.
Yes, it was.
My mouth gets exercise and my brain gets homework.
But in a good way.
Yes, in a useful way.
Let's think about what we learned.
First, we learned what shadowing is.
It means listening and repeating right after a speaker.
We used phrases like repeat after the speaker, copy the rhythm, and follow the sentence.
Then we talked about why shadowing helps beginners.
It improves pronunciation, listening, speaking speed, and confidence.
After that, we explained a simple practice method.
First, listen, then listen with the text, then repeat, then copy the feeling, and finally, say it alone.
We also said short practice is enough.
10 to 15 minutes can really help.
Then we talked about common mistakes.
We said learners often choose sentences that are too hard, move on too quickly, or focus only on speed.
Yes, and we learned that slow, clear practice is often smarter.
After that, we looked at real examples.
We practiced short daily sentences like I'm on my way, take your time, and I think I'll have tea.
Those are great because they work in real life.
Finally, we talked about habit.
Shadowing works best when you do it regularly and use sentences that match your life.
So, the big message is simple.
Don't try to be perfect, Try to be regular.
Exactly. Short, clear, daily practice can help you speak more naturally.
And day three is a great day to keep going.
Yes, you are building real progress one sentence at a time.
Now, we want to hear from you.
This is our favorite part.
Yes, because this is where you join the lesson, too.
Our question of the day is, what kind of English sentences do you want to shadow most?
And when do you want to practice them?
I'll answer first.
I want to shadow short daily conversation sentences.
I like them because I can use them with friends, at cafes, and when I travel.
That is a great choice.
My answer is a little different.
I want to shadow polite work and daily routine sentences because they help me sound clear and organized.
See, we have different answers, and that's okay.
So viewers, we want to know about you.
Maybe you like travel English.
Maybe you like greetings.
Maybe you like simple everyday routines.
Here are some example answers you can copy.
I want to shadow daily routine sentences because they are easy and useful.
I want to practice after dinner because my home is quiet then.
I want to shadow travel English because I want more confidence.
Please tell us in the comments.
Write, I want to shadow blank sentences because blank.
I practice at blank.
Or write, my favorite sentence to shadow is blank because blank.
You can also write, I practice English for blank minutes every day, and I want to improve my blank.
It helps us make better videos and helps you practice writing.
Yes, and when you write your plan, it becomes more real.
So, please share your answer with us.
Thank you so much for practicing English with us today.
We're really glad you spend your time here with us.
If this lesson helps you, give this video a big thumbs-up.
And click the subscribe button and the little bell.
That way, you won't forget to join us for the next lesson.
We have more speaking practice, listening practice, and useful daily English on the way.
You are all great students, and we are proud of your effort.
Keep practicing. Remember, short practice every day is stronger than one long practice once in a while.
Yes, one clear sentence today can become real confidence tomorrow.
And confidence sounds very good in English.
Have a wonderful day, evening, and night.
Keep speaking, keep smiling, and keep going.
Bye, everyone.
